title: Providence
hook: Calvin: nothing happens by chance; God holds all things

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's theology of the cross: God hidden where people don't think to look. Your line was God hidden in weakness.

Joseph's brothers stand in front of him in Egypt, terrified. Long ago they threw him into a pit and sold him. Now he's the man who decides whether their families eat. Their father has just died, and they're sure revenge is coming. Joseph weeps. Then he tells them: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." You heard that line back in year two. One event, two intentions inside it. John Calvin built a whole teaching on lines like that, under the name providence.

Calvin taught that nothing happens by chance. The world isn't a machine God wound up and walked away from, and it isn't a dice game either. God holds all things and steers them. He leaned on Jesus's words about sparrows sold in the market: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered." And on a proverb: "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD." Even a cast lot doesn't fall outside God's hand. For Calvin this wasn't a cold idea to argue about. He wrote that knowing God's providence brings thankfulness when things go well, patience when they don't, and freedom from anxiety about what's coming. If the future is in God's hand, he reasoned, a believer doesn't have to hold all of it alone. Christians understand providence in different ways. Reformed churches follow Calvin closely, with strong words about God's governing of every event. Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist and other Christians also confess God's providence, while describing human freedom and chance in their own ways. And they read the same Joseph. Notice when he says his line: not from the bottom of the pit, but years later, looking back over the whole road. Providence in Genesis is something Joseph sees in the rearview mirror. While it was happening, it only looked like a pit.

Bring to mind one thing you can't control, a test result, a decision someone else will make, a child far away, and notice how your hands want to grip it. Let them open on your lap. If you pray, hand that one thing to God, held in a hand bigger than yours; if you don't, notice what it's like to set it down for these two minutes.
Providence. Calvin's teaching that God holds and steers all things, so that nothing happens by chance.
Your line: held in his hand. Joseph saw it looking back. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Christians speak of God's providence in prayer and in hard times, often with Joseph's words from Genesis 50:20; Reformed churches teach it in Calvin's strong form, and other churches confess it while describing human freedom in their own ways.

options: Genesis has him say it years later, looking back: ye thought evil, but God meant it for good.
Yes. Genesis has him explain God's whole plan right there in the pit, as it happened.
No. Genesis says Joseph never forgave his brothers or saw any good in what happened.

notes: Calvin is paraphrased; the fruits of providence (gratitude, patience, freedom from worry about the future) follow Institutes I.17.7–11. Confirm.
Calvin's use of Matthew 10:29 and Proverbs 16:33 in Institutes I.16 should be confirmed.
The sentence on Catholic, Orthodox and Methodist views is deliberately general; confirm it is fair to each.
'Long ago' and 'years later' are left unquantified on purpose (Genesis gives the timeline only indirectly).
